subject: economics
title: Model Question Paper 3
meta: Time: 3 hours · Maximum marks: 100 · Modelled on the April 2026 NIOS paper
instructions: All questions are compulsory. Where a question has OR, answer either one.
Section A: questions 1–20 are MCQs (1 mark each). Section B: questions 21–35 have two parts of 1 mark each.
Section C: 2-mark answers in 30–50 words, 3-mark answers in 50–80 words, 5-mark answers in 80–120 words. Show the working in numerical questions.
Questions from previous NIOS papers show the exam they appeared in.

sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (fill in the blanks, true/false, match, one word or complete the table).

questions.q: State True or False: (a) We buy goods and services from the market. (b) The market is not flooded with goods today.
questions.answer:
(a) True.
(b) False — markets today are full of a wide variety of goods.

questions.q: State True or False: (a) A teacher teaching in a school is production. (b) Growing vegetables in a kitchen garden is not production.
questions.answer:
(a) True — a service is produced.
(b) False — it creates utility, so it is production.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: What are public goods? Give two examples you use.
questions.answer:
Public goods are owned and enjoyed by society as a whole and are available to everyone without discrimination.
Examples: roads, bridges, parks, street lights, a town hall.

questions.q: In what two ways is production disposed of?
questions.answer: Production is used for (1) consumption, the direct satisfaction of wants, and (2) capital formation, the part not consumed that is added to the stock of machines, buildings and so on to expand future production.

questions.q: What is division of labour?
questions.answer: Division of labour means splitting the production of a good into many processes and giving each process to the worker best suited to it. It raises efficiency and makes large-scale production possible.

or.answer: Working capital is the raw material used up in a single round of production, such as yarn, clay, seeds and fertilisers. Fixed capital, by contrast, lasts many years.

questions.q: Define fixed cost.
questions.answer: Fixed cost is the expenditure on fixed factors, such as rent for land or a tractor. It is compulsory and does not change with the amount of output; it must be paid even if nothing is produced.

or.q: What is meant by cost of production?
or.answer: Cost of production is the money expenditure a producer incurs to buy or hire factors of production (land, labour, capital) and raw materials to produce goods and services.

questions.q: What is a demand curve?
questions.answer: A demand curve is the diagram of the demand schedule. Price is on the Y-axis and quantity demanded on the X-axis. It slopes downward from left to right, showing the law of demand.

questions.q: How does improved technology affect supply?
questions.answer: Better technology lowers the cost of production per unit and raises the profit margin, so firms supply more of the commodity at the same price.

questions.q: Why was it difficult to equate the values of different goods under barter?
questions.answer: There was no common unit of measurement. A cow cannot be divided, and no one good could measure the value of all others, so it was hard to say how much cloth or grain equalled a cow.

questions.q: What is the meaning of banking?
questions.answer: Banking means accepting deposits of money from the public for lending or investment. The deposits are repayable on demand or otherwise and can be withdrawn by cheque, draft or order.

questions.q: Distinguish between direct personal investigation and indirect investigation.
questions.answer:
Direct: the investigator collects information personally from the respondents. It is reliable but open to personal bias.
Indirect: information is taken from third persons who know the facts. It is used by government commissions.

questions.q: State the purpose of an average.
questions.answer: An average gives a single value representative of all the items. It sums up large data briefly, makes comparison between groups easy, and helps in framing policy.

or.q: State two functions of an average.
or.answer:
(1) It presents raw data briefly in one representative figure.
(2) It makes comparison between two or more groups easy.

questions.q: Explain the right to safety.
questions.answer: Consumers have the right to protection against goods and services that are dangerous to health and life, such as adulterated food, spurious medicines and unsafe electrical goods.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: 'The larger the surplus, the larger the productive capacity of the economy.' Explain.
questions.answer:
The surplus is the part of production not consumed.
It is invested in capital goods such as plant, machinery and buildings, which is capital formation.
A larger surplus means more capital goods, so the economy can produce more in future.

questions.q: A shopkeeper sells 10 kg of rice at ₹30 a kg, or 11 kg at ₹29 a kg. Find AR in each case and MR.
questions.answer:
TR at 10 kg = 10 × 30 = ₹300, so AR = ₹30.
TR at 11 kg = 11 × 29 = ₹319, so AR = ₹29.
MR = 319 − 300 = ₹19.
AR equals the price; MR differs from AR because the price fell.

questions.q: How do climatic conditions affect market demand?
questions.answer:
Market demand changes with the season.
In summer, demand rises for ice, cold drinks, coolers and cotton clothes.
In the rainy season, demand rises for umbrellas and raincoats.
In winter, demand rises for woollens and heaters.
So the same good is in high demand in one season and low demand in another.

questions.q: Explain money as a standard of deferred payment with an example.
questions.answer:
Money is used to make payments in the future. A friend borrows ₹300 to buy a book and promises to repay it after a week with ₹1 interest, i.e. ₹301.
The lender accepts money because it keeps its value; a used book would not be accepted.
So loans and future payments are settled in money.

questions.q: Calculate the mean (discrete, short-cut): children 0–6 with families 13, 17, 20, 40, 20, 17, 13.
Distinguish between renewable and non-renewable resources with examples.
questions.answer:
Renewable resources are replenished naturally over time and can be used without running out if used carefully — forests, fish, water, solar and wind energy.
Non-renewable resources are exhausted as they are used and cannot be replaced — coal, petroleum, natural gas, minerals. They must be used carefully for future generations.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Write short notes on (a) the Reserve Bank of India and (b) cooperative banks.
questions.answer:
(a) RBI: the central bank and head of the banking system, with its headquarters in Mumbai. All banks follow its rules. It issues currency notes (except one-rupee notes and coins, which the Ministry of Finance issues) and acts as banker to the central and state governments.
(b) Cooperative banks: run by cooperative societies under state laws. Rural ones lend for farming, cattle and fishery; urban ones lend for self-employment, small industry, durable goods and personal finance. Examples are state cooperative banks, PACS, urban cooperative banks and land development banks.

questions.q: Explain the importance of the service sector in providing employment and promoting exports.
questions.answer:
Employment: the service sector employed 29.4% of workers in 2009–10, and this share is rising. Educated people (graduates, engineers, doctors, professionals) find jobs in banking, IT, transport, education and health. It pays more than agriculture and offers year-round, non-seasonal work.
Exports: India's business services — IT, consultancy and legal services — are of world standard and earned about ₹4.35 lakh crore of foreign exchange in 2009–10. The sector also attracts foreign direct investment, which creates still more jobs.
